## Objectives

By the end of this assignment, you will be able to:

- Time an operation that is far too fast to time directly, by repeating it
- Explain why the *minimum* of several measurements is closer to the truth than
  the average
- Read a growth class off a series of measurements, and write down the rule you
  used as code
- Explain why the geometric mean of a set of ratios is the right average and the
  ordinary one is not
- Say what `vector` and `list` are each good and bad at, and why
- Explain amortized constant time, and point at a measurement of it
- Say what a straight line on a log-log chart means, and what its slope is
- Defend a complexity claim from evidence rather than from memory

This assignment covers course skills **D1** (classify the Big-O of a code
snippet: here the snippets are the eight timing loops, and `findings.txt` is
where you classify them), **D2** (draw and compare growth curves) and **D3**
(best, worst and amortized), from cluster **D**, assessed at **Window 2** on
Nov 20. It is also where the linked-list-versus-dynamic-array comparison from
week 6 gets settled, with numbers.

## 1. Introduction

Since week 5 we have been saying what operations cost. A `vector` subscript
is O(1). Prepending to a vector is O(n). A linked list prepends in O(1), but
reaching its middle means walking there. Appending to a dynamic array is
amortized constant, O(1\*), because doubling makes the expensive append rare.

So far you have taken those on our word. In this assignment you measure them.

The tool is the stopwatch in `Timer.h`, which writes down the time before and
after. You time eight experiments at five container sizes each, and the growth
class of each one shows in how its times change from size to size.

::: {.callout-note}
**What is different about this assignment.** Everywhere else this semester there
has been a right answer sitting in a file somewhere, and the checks compare
against it. Here the numbers are different on every machine, at every moment,
and on a laptop with a browser open they will be different from one minute to
the next.

So what is graded is the reasoning that
turns numbers into a class, and that is the same everywhere. §5 is the code
version of it. §8 is the sentence version.
:::

## 4. Why You Cannot Just Time One Operation

A `vector` subscript takes less than a nanosecond. Asking the clock what time
it is takes far longer than that. So this:

```cpp
t.start();
sink += v[i];              // the thing we want to measure
double us = t.elapsed();   // almost entirely the cost of asking
```

measures the stopwatch, not the subscript.

Two techniques fix it, and both are already in the code you were given.

**Repeat, then divide.** Do the operation thousands of times between one
`start()` and one `elapsed()`, and divide by the count. The clock is read twice
in total rather than twice per operation. `repsFor(n)` in `given.cpp` gives the
count, twenty thousand at every size. It has to be the same at every size: the
clock's own cost gets divided by the count too, and a count that changed with n
would make that cost look like growth.

**Take the minimum, not the mean.** `measure()` runs each timing function five
times and keeps the *smallest* answer, for this reason:

::: {.callout-note}
Noise on a shared machine is **one-sided**. The operating system scheduling
something else, another student's compile starting up, a cache line being
evicted: each of those makes a measurement take **longer**. None of them makes
it shorter.

So the average of several runs is the true cost *plus* however much interference
there happened to be. The minimum is the true cost plus the interference in the
quietest run, and with enough runs, one of them lands in a quiet moment.
:::

There is one more fix, in `buildVector` in `given.cpp`; the comment there
explains it. The operating system hands over the memory of a large vector
lazily, the first time each part of it is written. Without a warm-up, the first
appends after building a million-element vector are charged for that, and an
O(1) operation measures as something else.

## 5. TODO 1, `classifyGrowth`

You can write and fully test this before
timing anything.

You are given the times at five sizes, where **each size is ten times the one
before**. The question is what shape they imply.

By eye, you would look at whether the time went up when n went up, and by how
much. If n grows tenfold and the time does not change, that is constant. If the
time also grows tenfold, that is linear. If it grows a hundredfold, quadratic.

| the time grows by, per tenfold step | the class |
|---|---|
| about 1×, it barely moves | `O(1)` |
| about 10× | `O(n)` |
| about 100× | `O(n²)` |

### The rule, exactly

1. **Refuse to guess.** Return `UNKNOWN` if `count < 2`, or any time is zero or
   negative, or any size is not exactly ten times the one before it.

2. Compute the ratio between each pair of neighboring times:

   ```cpp
   ratio[i] = times[i] / times[i-1];       // for i = 1 .. count-1
   ```

3. Take the **geometric mean** of those ratios, multiply them together and take
   the `(count-1)`-th root:

   ```cpp
   double growth = pow(product, 1.0 / (count - 1));
   ```

4. Read the class off that number, by whichever of 1, 10 and 100 it is
   nearest to:

   ```
   growth <  3.16  ->  CONSTANT
   growth < 31.6   ->  LINEAR
   otherwise       ->  QUADRATIC
   ```

::: {.callout-warning}
**`count` measurements have `count - 1` ratios**, so the root is the
`(count-1)`-th. Five measurements are four steps apart. Taking the fifth root
instead of the fourth is the single most common way to get this wrong, and it
does not fail loudly. It reclassifies a quadratic series as linear without
any error.
:::

### Why the geometric mean

Suppose a measurement is unlucky and comes out ten times too slow, and the
next one is normal. The ratios are 10 and 1/10.

The ordinary average of 10 and 1/10 is **5.05**, which says the time is growing
about linearly. It is not; it went up and came straight back down. The
geometric mean of 10 and 1/10 is `sqrt(10 × 1/10)` = **exactly 1**, which is
the truth.

Going up tenfold and coming back down tenfold should cancel, and only the
geometric mean makes them cancel. One of the checks is a series that jumps up
and back down four times, to catch an implementation that adds the ratios up and
divides.

The same property is what makes the rule survive real noise. A single
measurement that comes out 30% high moves the geometric mean of four ratios by
about 7%, nowhere near enough to cross a boundary.

::: {.callout-note}
**Where 3.16 and 31.6 come from.** A perfect O(1) series gives exactly 1, a
perfect O(n) series exactly 10, and a perfect O(n²) series exactly 100. Real
measurements never land exactly on any of them, so each goes to the nearest.
Because these are ratios, "nearest" means fewer times bigger or smaller:
3.16 is 3.16 times 1, and 10 is 3.16 times 3.16, so 3.16 sits halfway between
1 and 10. 31.6 sits halfway between 10 and 100 the same way. Real measured
values come out around 1.05 and 10.4, nowhere near a boundary.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Where is O(log n)?** Not in the rule, and not in any of the eight experiments.
From n = 100 to n = 1,000,000, log n goes from about 2 to 6. It triples while n
grows ten-thousandfold, about 1.3 times per tenfold step. That is nearer 1 than
10, so the rule calls it constant, and no stopwatch on a shared machine could do
better: noise alone moves a measurement more than that. This is the reason an
O(log n) operation, like binary search, feels as fast as a constant one in
practice.
:::

## 6. TODOs 2–6, The Five Timing Functions

Read `timeVectorSubscript` and `timeVectorAppend` in `Stopwatch.cpp` first. Both
follow the same five steps:

1. build a container of `n` items, **outside** the timer
2. ask `repsFor(n)` how many repetitions to do
3. start the timer
4. do the operation that many times
5. stop, and divide by the repetition count

The five you write are the same shape with a different operation in the middle.

Three of them use `list`, the standard library's linked list, from
`#include <list>`. It is the same idea as the `List` we wrote in class, with
`push_back`, `push_front` and iterators that work the way they do on a
`vector`. It has no `[]`, for the reason we saw in class: reaching the middle of
a list means walking there.

| TODO | Function | The operation |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | `timeListAppend` | `l.push_back(1)` |
| 3 | `timeVectorPrepend` | `v.insert(v.begin(), 1)` |
| 4 | `timeListPrepend` | `l.push_front(1)` |
| 5 | `timeVectorTraverse` | walk `begin()` to `end()` with an iterator |
| 6 | `timeListTraverse` | the same, on a list |

Three things to watch:

::: {.callout-warning}
**TODO 3 uses 50 repetitions, not `repsFor(n)`.** Two thousand prepends into a
vector of a million would move a hundred billion elements and you would still be
sitting there. Fifty is plenty to measure, and it grows the vector by so little
that n is still effectively n. The TODO comment says this too.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**TODOs 5 and 6 do not divide by n.** A traversal is already n operations; you
want to watch the cost of *one whole walk* grow. Divide by the repetition count
only. Dividing by n as well turns an O(n) measurement into a flat line, which is
a real answer to a different question.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**`vector` has no `push_front`.** Putting an element at the front of a vector
means moving every other element up one place, so the library does not offer it
as a one-word operation. `insert(v.begin(), value)` does it, and your
measurement shows what it costs.
:::

Now run it:

```bash
make
./stopwatch
```

Eight rows, five columns, and a class in the last column worked out by your own
`classifyGrowth`. Look at the table before moving on. Some rows deserve a
second look, and §8 is where you say why.

### Opening an HTML file that lives on Coder {#opening-html}

Your VS Code runs on your laptop, but your files live on the Coder server. So
double-clicking `results.html` in the Explorer just shows you the HTML source,
there is no browser on the far end to render it.

The fix is to serve the folder over HTTP and let VS Code bring the port back to
your laptop. In the VS Code terminal, from your repository folder:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000
```

VS Code notices the new listening port within a second or two and forwards it
automatically, you will see a notification, and a **PORTS** tab appears next to
the terminal. Now open this in your own browser:

```

```

Press **Ctrl-C** in the terminal to stop the server when you are done.

::: {.callout-tip}
`http://localhost:8000/sample-results.html` works right now, before you have

can see what the page looks like when it works, and what each of the four

You can also right-click a file in the Explorer and choose **Download…** to copy
it to your laptop and open it normally.
:::

### Reading a log-log chart

Both axes are logarithmic, which is the trick that makes shapes readable.

On ordinary axes, an O(n) curve and an O(n²) curve both look like "a line that
goes up steeply" and you cannot tell them apart. On log-log axes, **every power
law is a straight line, and the slope is the exponent**:

- `O(1)` is **flat**
- `O(n)` climbs at **45 degrees**, one decade up for one decade across
- `O(n²)` climbs at **twice** that
- `O(log n)` climbs, but **bends over**, it is the one line that is not straight

That is the same fact `classifyGrowth` computes. Its growth number is ten
raised to the slope, and the rule rounds the slope to 0, 1 or 2.

## 8. TODO 8, `findings.txt`

Eight lines, one per experiment: the name, the complexity class, and one
sentence saying why.

```
vector-subscript   O(1)   the index is arithmetic, size never enters in
```

The accepted spellings are `O(1)`, `O(1*)`, `O(logn)`, `O(n)` and `O(n^2)`,
none of them with a space inside. `O(1)*` and `O(lgn)` are accepted too. Lines
starting with `#` are ignored, so the instructions in the file can stay where
they are.

**Two of the eight deserve the asterisk.** `O(1*)` means *amortized* constant:
most operations are cheap, one in a while is expensive, and the average over
many is constant.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not just copy the last column of the table across.** Your `classifyGrowth`
reports what it measured, and a measurement cannot tell everything:

- **The asterisk does not show up on a stopwatch.** Every append row comes out
  O(1) in your table. Which of them are amortized depends on what happens on the
  rare append that finds no room, and you have to know that from how the
  container works. Read `timeVectorAppend` and `timeRepeatedVectorAppend`
  again, and ask whether a `list` ever has to copy anything when it grows.

- **Two rows are the same class as each other**, and at a million one of them is
  several times slower than the other. Both are `O(n)`. Big-Oh does not describe
  constant factors. Put the reason for the difference, where the elements
  physically are in memory, in your sentence.
:::

### What is graded here

1. All eight lines present, names spelled as the skeleton has them.
2. **The class on each line is right.** These are facts about the algorithms,
   not about your laptop, a fixed answer key, unaffected by hardware.
3. A reason of at least six words on each line. The wording is not marked, but
   a line without a reason fails.

If a class you measured disagrees with the class you can argue for from first
principles, write down the one you can argue for, and then work out why the
measurement disagreed.

::: {.callout-important}
**None of these checks grade your milliseconds.** Not one of them compares a
timing against a target number, because the grading machine is shared and your
laptop is not it.

The harness group only asks whether the experiment *ran*: eight rows, five
sizes, every time greater than zero, the linear ones visibly growing and the
constant ones visibly not. Everything else is checked against things that are
the same on every computer.
:::

Every failure comes with a hint. Finish §5 first. Sixteen of the
thirty-six pass without any timing code at all.

::: {.callout-tip}
Focus on one check while you are fixing it:

```bash
make checks
./checks "Classify: a flat series is constant"
./checks "Classify: a series that jumps up and back down has no trend"
```

A test name needs the full name, or a prefix with a `*` on the end. `./checks
"Classify:"` matches nothing, prints almost nothing, and exits successfully,
which looks a lot like passing.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**There are no hidden tests.** What you run with `make test` is exactly what the
grader runs, all 36 checks. If it passes here, it passes there.

Grading always runs the official copies of `test.py` and `checks.cpp`, not the
